examnote: Medians over dams; 90 % bootstrap interval of the pilot's median J: 0.0097–0.0202 (SOP 0.089–0.134). The pilot beats SOP on 206 of 244 dams (84 %) and the historical operations on 95 %; the perfect-foresight DP beats the pilot on 70 %. On the 151 dams whose records close the mass balance (B's subset): pilot 0.016, SOP 0.099, DP 0.007. The tuned flood-pool rule is the strongest classical comparator: same simulations, 3 parameters, no network. Its g4-tuned version is shown; the g1-tuned one scored 0.029. Storage columns are fractions of capacity; "end − start" is the storage change over the scored window.
scatnote: Each dot is one exam dam (log axes, clipped to 0.0001–3). Below the dashed line, the pilot's J is lower than SOP's (blue: 206 dams); above it, higher (orange: 37 dams). Many SOP failures sit at the right edge: dams where SOP spills far above Qmax.
losses:
Large reservoirs in a drier decade. The pilot loses to SOP on 37 dams (15 %). Their median capacity is 2.0 years of inflow, against 0.7 for the dams where it wins. Their scored decade carried 0.80 of the calibration decade's inflow, against 0.87. Most are irrigation or water-supply dams (24 of 37). On dams whose scored decade was more than 20 % drier, the pilot loses 20 % of the time; otherwise 12 %.

It keeps the lake lower. The cost J charges nothing for storage, so the pilot holds flood space: its median storage is 38 % of capacity, against 59 % for SOP and 68 % for DP. On 34 % of dams it ends the window at least 20 % of capacity lower than it started (SOP: 21 %). A real operator who values head for hydropower or a drought reserve would not accept that, and J does not see it. Its median end-minus-start change is +0.8 %, so it does not empty the lake as a rule.

More small floods, far fewer large ones. It goes above Qmax on 2.9 days a year (median), against 2.2 for SOP. Its median worst excess is 4 % of Qmax, against 96 % for SOP: it spreads a flood over several days of slightly too much water instead of one big spill. Under J's squared penalty that is the cheaper choice. Downstream, it may not be.

Still far from foresight. The perfect-foresight DP is 2.5 times lower (0.0063), and better on 70 % of dams. Most of that gap is information the pilot can't have: the timing of next month's storms.
ratchetnote: S<sub>J</sub> columns are the frozen simulated sets of generator g1 and g4. The decision column is the one re-taken in order on g4, the final frozen set. On g1 at the time, r3 and r4 were kept (S<sub>J</sub> 0.876 and 0.896). On g4 they fall below r2, because a network trained on stationary, noise-free inflows trusts its climatology too much. Not shown: two void runs whose training script never applied the optimiser step (found and fixed), and a first objective with a hard end-storage penalty inside one-year windows that punished natural seasonal drawdown (replaced by the one-year SOP tail). The c-rungs are the classical rule without a network.
genlist:
• Ranges from dev and aux dams only. Capacity, Qmax, demand and inflow statistics come from the 15 dev dams plus the 6 auxiliary dams with complete records. WaterData allows aux dams for calibration; they are never scored.
  • g2, gauge noise. Real ResOpsUS inflow is mostly back-calculated from storage changes, so it carries the storage gauge's error, differenced. On dev and aux dams, a median of 2 % of days have negative inflow, and up to 35 % on some dams. Half of the simulated dams get this noise.
  • g3, upstream dams and data spikes. 30 % of simulated inflows pass through an upstream reservoir first. 10 % get gross spikes; one dev dam has a 5×10⁹ m³/s day.
  • g4, a different decade. The twin test found the biggest gap. Smoothing the noise out of dev inflows barely changed the pilot's J (0.0361 → 0.0359). But on dev dams the scored half carried only 0.81 of the first half's mean inflow (median; 29 aux dams: 1.17). A stationary simulator gives about 1. Demand and climatology come from the first half, so a policy that trusts them over-releases in a drier decade. g4 scales the scored decade by exp(N(0, 0.3)).
  • After g4, SOP, rule curve and DP on the simulated frozen set have median J 0.105, 0.165 and 0.0069. B's real exam medians are 0.108, 0.143 and 0.0063. Those were published in the brief beforehand, but nothing was tuned to match them.
limits: J values only shortage and flooding. The pilot exploits that: it keeps reservoirs low (median storage 38 % of capacity against SOP's 59 %). Under an objective that counted head, carry-over storage or recreation, it would need retraining.

It loses to SOP on 15 % of exam dams, mostly large irrigation and supply reservoirs whose scored decade was drier than the decade their demand was taken from. On 34 % of dams it ends at least 20 % of capacity lower than it started.
The perfect-foresight DP is still 2.5× lower. The pilot uses no inflow forecast; an MPC with a forecaster is the natural next step.
One reservoir at a time: no cascades, no coordinated systems, no evaporation (the benchmark ignores it), no minimum environmental flow, and demand is a fixed day-of-year calendar.
Inflow records are back-calculated and noisy; 93 of 244 exam dams do not close their mass balance. The pilot's median on the 151 that do is about the same (0.016).
The CDEC recent exam has 15 dams; its interval is wide (pilot median 0.019, 90 % interval 0.0002–0.055).
